510	The custom of the Sephardim, the custom of the Eastern communities,
511	is to begin the Kinot on the night of Tisha beAv with the lament
512	of Haazinu.
513	Yes, even before the other Kinot they begin
514	to read the lament of Haazinu, the terrible prophecies of destruction
515	that Moshe Rabbeinu said. The lament of Haazinu foretells
516	evil days, hard days that even the greatest prophets of destruction
517	did not foresee the like of. Moshe Rabbeinu says verses
518	that are difficult even to repeat. He quotes
519	the Holy One, blessed be He: I said, days will come when the Holy One,

522	Israel to the corners of the world, one Jew here, one Jew
523	there, so that they lose completely their significance. Grain
524	that is gathered together, that is amassed, has importance, has
525	weight, has volume, has meaning. But

533	Days will come when the Holy One, blessed be He, will want to wipe out
534	the people of Israel, not only the body, heaven forbid, but

543	"I will not wipe out the people of Israel" only so as not to let

548	Let us imagine terrible and dreadful things. There are no other
549	prophecies as harsh and terrible as the lament of
550	Haazinu. And here a question arises: so why is this a song?
551	Why is Haazinu a song and not a lament? On the night of Tisha beAv
552	the Eastern communities read it as a lament,
553	but all year round it is a song. First, in the Torah itself it
554	is written in verse form. Second, it is written like two
555	columns with a break in the middle, the way a song is written. Third,
556	in the Beit HaMikdash the Levites would sing it, literally
557	with song and melody. Every Shabbat they would sing "Hazeiv lecha."
558	"Hazeiv lecha" means they would divide the song of Haazinu
559	into six parts, and every Shabbat they would sing one part.
560	Accordingly, in the synagogue we divide
561	the first part of Haazinu into six aliyot. "Hazeiv lecha":
562	"Give ear, O heavens, and I will speak; remember the days of old, understand
563	the years of generations." We divide the song of Haazinu into six
564	parts
565	and read the first six aliyot the way
566	the Levites would sing in the Beit HaMikdash. They sing for six Shabbatot
567	and then start over again. How can we
568	leave out what the Levites sang? "I said I would scatter them":
569	with what melody did they sing it? These are, after all,
570	terrible prophecies of exile, which one should read
571	sitting on the ground on Tisha beAv night,
572	and the Levites would sing suffering, sing pain. A huge question
573	lies here: is Haazinu a song or is Haazinu
574	a lament? How can we understand this whole matter?
575	The Rebbe once said something truly brilliant in Likutei Sichot,
576	in a short note he said it, but it is truly something
577	so special.
578	Haazinu is a song because it films the entire path.
579	Haazinu is a song because it is a panoramic picture
580	of all the chapters of all the episodes in the life of the people of
581	Israel. Haazinu, says the Ramban, depicts past, present,
582	and future. In the song of Haazinu, the suffering, the pain, the
583	terrible lament is a chapter
584	within the great plan that leads to the redemption.
585	And over this a Jew sings: not over this moment, but over the understanding
586	that this moment produces redemption, produces good,
587	produces a greatness that the good days did not produce.
588	A Jew does not sing over this moment as it is, but over
589	this moment as it is part of the movement of the train, part
